newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal government survives, but still seen in crisis.
newsitem.headline: Nepal government survives, but still seen in crisis.

text.p: Nepal's centre-right government, which narrowly survived a vote of no-confidence this week, remains in crisis because junior partners in the coalition are in disarray, politicians and analysts said on Wednesday.
The vote gave the Himalayan kingdom only temporary relief from its fluid politics, and raised fresh questions on the future of its fledgling democracy, they said.
"The government has run into a minority," said Madhav Kumar Nepal, the powerful general secretary of the main opposition Unified Marxist Leninst (UML) party.
"It has no right to remain in power. The political crisis has now begun," he said. "
The UML garnered enough support from other parties to secure 101 votes compared with the 15-month-old government's 84.

But Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's three-party coalition survived because the constitution requires a majority vote of the total lower house -- 103 of the 205 members -- to carry a no-confidence motion against the government.
Deuba told Reuters after Tuesday's vote that he hoped the rifts within his coalition could be resolved and that he planned to work more closely with the opposition.
Voting on the motion took place without five government ministers who were sent to Bangkok for medical treatment.
Opposition lawmakers said the government kept them away for fear they would turn against it. Deuba denied any wrongdoing.

"It is a temporary solace for the government. The type of politicking that has evolved raises a serious question for the future of Nepali democracy," said Sridhar Khatri, political scientist at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan University.
The five ministers who were away in Bangkok belonged to the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), a key coalition partner of Deuba's Nepali Congress party.
The no-confidence motion was prompted by a split in the RPP, whose breakaway leaders have alleged the government has attempted to harass its workers.
Deuba has also lost the support of two members of the Nepal Sadhavana Party, the third party in the coalition.
The communists had offered to back Lokendra Bahadur Chand, who heads the breakaway group from the RPP, as prime minister if the motion had passed.
Nine of the RPP's 19 deputies in parliament voted with the UML party for the motion, which was also supported by other small leftist parties.
The RPP is considered close to Nepal's monarchy, which yielded its absolute powers to allow a multi-party democracy in 1990 under a constitutional monarchy.
This followed a bloody pro-democracy movement spearheaded by the Nepali Congress party.
The UML's Nepal said Deuba should either seek a vote of confidence in parliament to show a majority or resign.
Party leaders were expected to decide their future course of action on Thursday.
Deuba came to power in September 1995, replacing a UML government through a no confidence motion. He survived a similar move against him in March this year.
"It (the defeat of the motion) gives a temporary relief to the prime minister to think about a new course for the future," said Parliamentary Affairs Minister Narahari Acharya.
